content: Constipation is a prevalent issue in children, and osmotic and stimulant laxatives are commonly used to manage this condition. However, there has been a lack of high-quality evidence to support their efficacy and safety. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of these laxatives in treating functional constipation in children. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, up to March 10, 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children aged 0 to 18 years were included. The primary outcome assessed was the frequency of defecation, while secondary outcomes included fecal incontinence, disimpaction, the need for additional therapies, and adverse events. Twenty-five RCTs involving 2,310 participants were included in the analysis. Fourteen of these studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias due to issues such as lack of blinding, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting. A meta-analysis of two studies (101 participants) comparing polyethylene glycol (PEG) with placebo demonstrated a significant increase in the number of stools per week with PEG (mean difference [MD] 2.61 stools per week, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15 to 4.08). Common adverse events in these placebo-controlled studies included flatulence, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, and headache. Higher doses of PEG (0.7 g/kg) resulted in significantly more stools per week compared to lower doses (0.3 g/kg) (1 study, 90 participants, MD 1.30, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.84). When comparing PEG to lactulose in six studies (465 participants), PEG was associated with a significantly greater number of stools per week (MD 0.70, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.31). Additionally, fewer patients receiving PEG required additional laxative therapies (18% vs. 31%, risk ratio [RR] 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.83). No serious adverse events were reported for either agent, though common side effects included diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and pruritus ani. In three studies (211 participants) comparing PEG with milk of magnesia, PEG was associated with a slightly higher number of stools per week (MD 0.69, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89). However, the clinical significance of this difference was considered small. One child was reported to have an allergic reaction to PEG, but no other serious adverse events were noted. In one study, milk of magnesia was found to be superior to lactulose in terms of stool frequency (MD -1.51, 95% CI -2.63 to -0.39, 50 participants). Two studies (287 participants) comparing liquid paraffin (mineral oil) with lactulose showed a significant increase in stool frequency with liquid paraffin (MD 4.94, 95% CI 4.28 to 5.61). Adverse events included abdominal pain, distension, and watery stools, but no serious adverse events were reported. No significant differences in stool frequency were observed in comparisons between PEG and enemas, dietary fiber mixes, senna, lactitol, hydrolyzed guar gum, flixweed, or liquid paraffin in various smaller studies. The authors concluded that PEG appears to be more effective than placebo, lactulose, and milk of magnesia for managing childhood constipation. However, the overall quality of evidence was rated as low or very low due to methodological limitations, heterogeneity, and short follow-up periods. Liquid paraffin also showed evidence of efficacy. There was no evidence to suggest that lactulose is superior to other agents studied. Further research is needed to explore the long-term use of PEG, the role of liquid paraffin, and the optimal dosing of PEG for childhood constipation.
